lessons.title: Dusting the Phone — Jackie Kay
lessons.description: Jackie Kay's speaker waits anxiously by the phone in this portrait of obsessive modern love.
lessons.content_html:
Dusting the Phone — Jackie Kay

Jackie Kay’s “Dusting the Phone” captures the agony of waiting for a lover to call. Written as a single, spiralling monologue, the poem takes place entirely inside the speaker’s head as she swings between hope and dread. The named poem is printed on the exam paper, so for the specified-poem question you can quote directly from it; for the comparison question no text is given beyond a list of titles, so you must learn short quotations from your chosen second poem and know which poems pair well with this one.

The Poem’s Situation

The poem opens with brutal honesty. The speaker admits she is “imagining the worst that could happen”, even though she knows this is “not a good idea”. She recognises that being in love should mean dwelling on “the best that has been happening” instead, but her anxious mind will not cooperate. This gap between what she should feel and what she actually feels sets up the poem’s central tension.

Key Fact

Kay builds anxiety through repetition and contradiction. Whether the phone rings or stays silent, the outcome feels equally threatening: the phone rings “heralding some disaster”, but “it doesn’t ring which also means disaster” too — both possibilities end in the single word “Sirens”, repeated twice. The speaker cannot escape her fear whatever happens.

The uncertainty spreads beyond the phone itself. The speaker imagines a chaotic set of possible futures, described through a comma-less list: “A marriage. A full house.” and time spent “in stranger’s white sheets”. She pictures “the future” as “a long gloved hand” and “an empty cup” — strange, ominous images with no clear meaning, mirroring racing thoughts that jump from one possibility to the next without pause.

Jackie Kay — Poet and Context

Jackie Kay (born 1961) is a Scottish poet and novelist. She served as the National Poet for Scotland, known as the Makar, between 2016 and 2021. Kay’s poetry is known for its warm, conversational voice and its honest exploration of relationships, identity and belonging. “Dusting the Phone” uses this same direct, everyday language to explore an experience many readers recognise: the powerlessness of waiting for someone to make contact.

Themes: Obsession and the Fragility of Modern Love

The poem is a dramatic monologue, spoken by the anxious lover from start to finish. Kay explores how love can tip into obsession: the speaker admits “I am trapped in it. I can’t move.” and wants her lover “all the time”. These short, blunt sentences contrast with the poem’s earlier long, breathless lines, capturing how obsessive thoughts can suddenly stop the speaker in her tracks.

Key Fact

The telephone becomes an object of near-religious devotion. The speaker calls her care of it “silver service”, then says “I polish it. I dress for it.” This extended metaphor of ceremonial preparation shows how far normal behaviour has been distorted by longing — an ordinary household object has become an altar.

Elsewhere the speaker’s desperation becomes almost comic and unsettling: she “assault[s] the postman for a letter” and “look[s] for flowers”, desperate for any sign of affection. Even unwanted contact is agony — “infuriatingly, it sends me hoaxes, wrong numbers” — because every call that is not from her lover is a fresh disappointment. When her lover’s voice does come, it “disappears into my lonely cotton sheets”, suggesting that even contact cannot fully satisfy her loneliness.

Kay writes in free verse, avoiding rhyme or a fixed rhythm so the poem sounds like a spontaneous, spiralling stream of thought. Frequent enjambment — for example “Your voice / disappears into my lonely cotton sheets” and “One night per week / in stranger’s white sheets” — mimics thoughts tumbling over one another without control, while the clipped, end-stopped fragments on a single line (“The future is a long gloved hand. An empty cup.”) jolt the reader from one image to the next. Kay also uses asyndeton in short, unlinked statements like “A marriage. A full house.”, speeding up the pace and suggesting panic. The poem is structurally circular: it opens with the speaker imagining disaster and ends with an unanswered demand — “Come on, damn you, ring me” — followed by “I don’t know what”, showing that her anxious cycle has no resolution.

“Dusting the Phone” pairs well with Elizabeth Barrett Browning’s “Sonnet 29”, because both poems show a speaker consumed by obsessive thoughts about a lover. Browning’s speaker admits her thoughts “twine and bud” around her lover like wild vines, wanting his real presence rather than her imagination of him. Kay’s speaker is similarly trapped by her own thoughts, though her tone is far more anxious than Browning’s calm confidence — a useful contrast for the comparison question.

The poem also compares well with Christina Rossetti’s “Cousin Kate”, since both present women left powerless by love. Rossetti’s speaker has been abandoned by “a great lord” and can only “howl in dust” over her situation, while Kay’s speaker waits helplessly for a phone call she cannot control. Both poems capture how love can strip a woman of agency, though Rossetti’s speaker suffers a public betrayal while Kay’s speaker’s suffering is private and psychological.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When answering on “Dusting the Phone”, use short, exact quotations — two or three words embedded in your own sentence are more reliable than a long quotation you might misremember in a closed-book exam. For the comparison question, organise your answer around methods (form, language, structure) rather than working through each poem separately: for example, discuss how both Kay’s free verse and your chosen comparison poem’s form reflect the speaker’s state of mind. Always explain the effect of a technique, not just name it.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Kay uses free verse, enjambment and asyndeton to mimic anxious, racing thoughts about an absent lover.
  • The telephone becomes an extended metaphor for obsession — the speaker “polishes” and “dresses” for it as if it were sacred.
  • The poem pairs well with “Sonnet 29” (obsessive love) and “Cousin Kate” (powerlessness in love) for the comparison question.

lessons.title: Remains — Simon Armitage
lessons.description: Armitage's soldier haunted by a looter he shot in 'Remains' — guilt, trauma and memory that will not stay behind.
lessons.content_html:
Remains — Context and the Soldier’s Voice

Simon Armitage based ‘Remains’ on real testimony from a soldier interviewed for The Not Dead, a documentary poetry project exploring the psychological damage that war leaves on veterans of conflicts including Bosnia, the Gulf War and Iraq. Rather than imagining war from a distance, Armitage worked directly from what the soldier told him, keeping close to the rhythms of everyday speech. The poem is written as a dramatic monologue, giving voice to a soldier who cannot escape one particular killing.

The Poem’s Story

The soldier describes being sent to stop looters raiding a bank. One man runs, “probably armed, possibly not,” and the soldier and two colleagues open fire: “Well myself and somebody else and somebody else” all shoot together. The looter is left “sort of inside out,” and a colleague “tosses his guts back into his body” before he is “carted off in the back of a lorry.” Armitage signals immediately that this will not be a simple war story: “End of story, except not really.”

Key Fact

The phrase “probably armed, possibly not” appears early in the poem and returns later in a slightly altered form during the soldier’s sleepless nights: “he’s probably armed, and possibly not.” The comma splitting the phrase is a stark caesura that mirrors the soldier’s own uncertainty — he never knows for sure that the looter was a genuine threat, and that doubt is what haunts him.

The looter’s death refuses to stay in the past. His “blood-shadow stays on the street,” and the soldier walks over it “week after week” while on patrol. Even at home, memory intrudes: he blinks and the man “bursts again through the doors of the bank.” Armitage uses enjambment to spill one memory into the next, showing how the soldier’s mind cannot contain or control the trauma.

Themes: Guilt and a Trauma That Will Not Leave

The soldier cannot separate what he did on duty from what he carries home. Sleep brings no rest: “Sleep, and he’s probably armed, and possibly not. / Dream, and he’s torn apart by a dozen rounds.” Even “the drink and the drugs” fail to remove the memory. The repeated present participles and unfinished thoughts show a mind stuck in replay, unable to reach any conclusion or resolution. The poem’s final line collapses past and present, killer and victim, into one image: “his bloody life in my bloody hands.”

Key Fact

The poem ends “his bloody life in my bloody hands,” repeating the word “bloody” as both a swear word of frustration and a literal description of blood on his hands. This refrain-like repetition captures how ordinary language cannot hold the weight of what he has done.

Armitage writes in loose, unrhymed stanzas that mimic natural speech, reflecting the poem’s roots in a real soldier’s spoken testimony. The tone is colloquial — phrases like “Well myself and somebody else and somebody else” and “Three of a kind all letting fly” sound like an unscripted, halting account rather than crafted poetry. This makes the horror feel closer to a confession than to literature.

The structure moves through time — from the shooting, to daily patrols, to being “home on leave,” to sleepless nights — showing that trauma does not stay contained to the battlefield. The final stanza drops all distance and addresses the moment directly: “near to the knuckle, here and now.”

‘Remains’ pairs naturally with Kamikaze by Beatrice Garland. Both poems explore how a single act connected to war leaves lasting damage — the kamikaze pilot lives with the shame of returning alive, while Armitage’s soldier lives with the guilt of a killing he cannot forget. 'Kamikaze' ends by suggesting death might have been easier than the living death of rejection — 'he must have wondered / which had been the better way to die' — while 'Remains' ends instead on inescapable personal guilt: 'his bloody life in my bloody hands.'

It also compares well with War Photographer by Carol Ann Duffy. Both speakers are trained to face violence — a soldier, a photographer — yet both are shown struggling to process what they have witnessed once they return to ordinary life. Duffy’s photographer is left staring back at his own memories; Armitage’s soldier cannot stop the looter bursting back into his.

A third pairing is Disabled by Wilfred Owen. Both poems show men permanently changed by conflict, but they handle time differently: Owen contrasts his soldier's present with an ordinary past of football and dances before his injury, while Armitage's soldier has no such refuge — the killing follows him from patrol ('out on patrol / I walk right over it week after week') into life at home ('Then I'm home on leave. But I blink').

Why This Matters for the Exam

For the specified-poem question, focus on how the caesura in “probably armed, possibly not,” the enjambment carrying memories forward, and the final repeated “bloody” work together to show guilt intruding into everyday life. For the comparison question, use Kamikaze, War Photographer or Disabled to discuss how different poets explore the long-term psychological cost of conflict, and note that Armitage’s colloquial, dramatic-monologue form is distinctive — it makes trauma sound like unfiltered testimony rather than crafted verse.
lessons.exam_tip_html: This is a closed-book exam, so memorise short, exact quotations rather than whole lines — “probably armed, possibly not,” “sort of inside out” and “bloody life in my bloody hands” are all compact enough to recall precisely under pressure. If ‘Remains’ is the specified poem, spend real time on form and structure, not just content — examiners reward comment on caesura, enjambment and the colloquial voice. If it appears in the comparison question, choose a partner poem you know well (Kamikaze, War Photographer or Disabled) and plan your comparison around shared methods, not just shared subject matter.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • ‘Remains’ is a dramatic monologue based on real soldier testimony, using colloquial language and caesura to show doubt and guilt.
  • Enjambment and repeated phrases (“probably armed, possibly not”) show memory intruding uncontrollably into the present.
  • The final line, “his bloody life in my bloody hands,” fuses guilt and literal violence, and pairs well with Kamikaze, War Photographer or Disabled in the comparison question.

lessons.title: Origin Story — Eve L. Ewing
lessons.description: How Eve L. Ewing turns her parents' first meeting into a comic-book myth about love, identity and memory.
lessons.content_html:
Origin Story — Love as a Myth We Tell Ourselves

Origin Story tells the tale of how the speaker’s parents met — not as a plain memory, but as a myth shaped like a comic book. The poem opens with the words “This is true”, immediately raising the question of what “true” means when a family story has been retold so many times it starts to feel invented. Eve L. Ewing borrows the structure of a comic-book origin story to explore how families turn ordinary beginnings into legend.

Poet and Context

Eve L. Ewing sets the poem in Chicago in the mid-1980s, where her parents “met at the Greyhound bus station”. The poem borrows the language of comic books — an origin story in comics explains how a hero began. By titling the poem “Origin Story”, Ewing treats her parents’ meeting with the same reverence a comic gives a superhero’s first transformation, elevating an everyday event into something mythic.

Key Fact

Ewing individualises her parents through vivid, contrasting details. Her mother is “thick glass and afro puff”, came west by train at nineteen, and “played tambourine in a Chaka Khan cover band”. Her father is “sleeveless and soft eye”, “ran away from home” at seventeen, and “mimeographed communist newspapers”. These specific, unglamorous facts root the myth in real working lives before the poem turns to comic-book imagery.

The turning point of the story is small and ordinary: her father sold comic books he had drawn himself for “one dollar”, and “my mother bought one”. This single transaction becomes the seed of the whole family. Ewing lets the everyday detail carry enormous weight — love begins not with fireworks but with a dollar and a drawing.

Ewing writes in free verse, with no rhyme and irregular line lengths, giving the poem a conversational, storytelling voice. Frequent enjambment lets sentences spill across lines — the phrase “never meant to last” flows straight out of the line before it, mirroring how a story keeps unfolding rather than stopping neatly. The poem has two movements: first, the narrative of the parents’ meeting; second, an extended reflection on what that story means for love itself. The shift is marked by the line “love is like a comic book”, where narrative turns into argument.

Themes: Fragility, Memory and Identity

The opening claim “This is true” sets up a tension the whole poem explores: is this history, or is it myth? Ewing does not resolve the question. Instead, she shows that families need myths — polished, retold versions of ordinary events — to hold their history together. The comic-book framing suggests that identity itself can be an extended metaphor: something drawn, collected and passed down rather than simply lived.

Key Fact

Ewing extends the comic-book metaphor across several lines: “love is like a comic book. it’s fragile”, and later, more starkly, “love is paper”. A cherished comic gets “curled into a back pocket” and “read under covers” until it is “worn thin, staples rusted”. Love, like the comic, survives only through careful, imperfect handling — and even when it wears out, the poem insists it “has a good ending”.

Cultural identity runs quietly through the poem’s details. The mother’s “afro puff” and her place in a “Chaka Khan cover band” root the story in Black American culture and music, while the father’s “mimeographed communist newspapers” hint at a countercultural, politically engaged background. These small, specific facts matter because they resist the glossy simplicity of an actual comic-book hero’s backstory — Ewing’s parents are real, complicated people before they become characters in her origin myth.

Comparisons with Other Anthology Poems

Catrin by Gillian Clarke also uses an extended metaphor for a family bond — the “red rope of love” connecting mother and daughter, echoing their “fierce confrontation”. Both poems show love as something physical and imperfect rather than simply sentimental, though Clarke focuses on ongoing conflict while Ewing looks back at how love began.

Sonnet 29 by Elizabeth Barrett Browning uses a different extended metaphor for love — the speaker’s thoughts as “wild vines, about a tree”, with the beloved as the tree (“O my palm-tree”) — to explore presence and absence. Where Browning wants her lover physically present rather than just imagined, Ewing is happy for her parents’ story to exist partly as imagined myth, showing two different attitudes to how love should be represented in words.

Kamikaze by Beatrice Garland also retells a parent’s history to the next generation, “recounting it later to her children”. Both poems explore how family stories are passed down and reshaped by the people who tell them, though Garland’s story carries the weight of shame and silence, while Ewing’s carries warmth and humour.

For the comparison question, Origin Story works well whenever the specified poem also uses an extended metaphor to explore love or family, or whenever a poem explores how personal or family history gets retold across generations. Examiners reward candidates who can identify the shared method — metaphor, narrative retelling, or structural shift from story to reflection — rather than just noting a shared topic.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When the comparison question pairs “Origin Story” with another poem, do not just say both poems are “about love” — compare the actual methods. Ewing builds her argument through an extended metaphor (comic book as love) layered onto a narrative structure, and short quotations like “love is paper” or “worn thin, staples rusted” are easy to memorise and analyse precisely. Remember that one anthology poem is printed on the paper, but the poem you choose to compare it with is not — so practise recalling two or three short, exact quotations for each poem you might choose, rather than vague paraphrases — examiners reward accurate embedded quotation far more than a general summary of the poem’s content.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Ewing frames her parents’ meeting as a comic-book “origin story”, blurring the line between true memory and family myth.
  • The extended metaphor of love as a fragile, well-worn comic book runs through the poem’s second half, from “it’s fragile” to “a good ending”.
  • Free verse and enjambment give the poem a conversational, storytelling voice that suits its theme of retelling family history.
